claims.source: Interestingly, we also found that the rescue of charged tRNAGln by CB-839 was accompanied by the uncharging of initiator and elongator tRNAMet species, as well as a reduced charging of several other tRNAs, which might indicate that tRNAMet is the second-most limiting tRNA class in MEFs subjected to amino acid deprivation.
claims.evidence: Supported by CHARGE-seq data in Figure 2C showing changes in tRNAMet and other tRNA charging with CB-839.

claims.claim: tRNAMet may be the second-most limiting tRNA class in MEFs subjected to amino acid deprivation.
claims.source: Interestingly, we also found that the rescue of charged tRNAGln by CB-839 was accompanied by the uncharging of initiator and elongator tRNAMet species, as well as a reduced charging of several other tRNAs, which might indicate that tRNAMet is the second-most limiting tRNA class in MEFs subjected to amino acid deprivation.
claims.evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observation that tRNAMet becomes uncharged when tRNAGln is restored.

claims.claim: GLS inhibition had only a marginal effect on GCN2 phosphorylation in MEFs deprived of amino acids for 6 hr.
claims.source: Consistent with the observed CB-839-triggered depletion of charged tRNAMet, GLS inhibition had only a marginal effect on GCN2 phosphorylation in MEFs deprived of amino acids for 6 hr (Figure 2E), or when cells were cultured for 24 hr in a 5% amino acid DMEM formulation, in which each amino acid contained in standard DMEM was supplied at a fraction equaling 5% of that in DMEM (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 2E showing minimal change in GCN2 phosphorylation with CB-839.

claims.claim: A498 and MiaPaCa2 cell lines show selective depletion of tRNAGln when deprived of extracellular amino acids that can be recovered by treatment with CB-839.
claims.source: As presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, A498, a renal cell line, and MiaPaCa2, a pancreatic cell line, show selective depletion of tRNAGln when deprived of extracellular amino acids that can be recovered by treatment with CB-839 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: Supported by tRNA charging assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and 1B showing tRNAGln depletion and rescue with CB-839.

claims.claim: In MiaPaCa2 cells, uncharging of tRNAArg was detected when tRNAGln charging was restored.
claims.source: Instead, uncharging of tRNAArg was detected in MiaPaCa2 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), but not in A498 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by tRNA charging assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B showing tRNAArg uncharging in MiaPaCa2.

claims.claim: The limiting nature of various charged tRNA pools may be dictated by the cellular context and differences in metabolism of individual amino acids in these cells.
claims.source: These observations indicate that the limiting nature of various charged tRNA pools may be dictated by the cellular context and differences in metabolism of individual amino acids in these cells.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that different cell types show different patterns of compensatory tRNA uncharging.

claims.claim: The specific loss of charged tRNAMet in amino-acid-deprived MEFs upon restoring the charged form of tRNAGln could be potentially explained by the critical role of methionine in S-adenosyl-methionine (SAM) production in support of cellular methylation and glutathione production through the transsulfuration pathway.
claims.source: The specific loss of charged tRNAMet in amino-acid-deprived MEFs upon restoring the charged form of tRNAGln could be potentially explained by the critical role of methionine in S-adenosyl-methionine (SAM) production in support of cellular methylation and glutathione production through the transsulfuration pathway (Zhu et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Speculative explanation based on known metabolic roles of methionine, supported by citation.

claims.claim: MiaPaCa2 is deficient for argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS1), and is, as a result, an arginine auxotroph.
claims.source: This finding may indicate that arginine is more profoundly limiting in amino-acid-depleted MiaPaCa2 cells than even methionine. This effect could be explained by the fact that MiaPaCa2, as are many other PDAC-derived lines, is deficient for argininosuccinate synthetase (ASS1), and is, as a result, an arginine auxotroph (Singh et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Singh et al., 2019 describing ASS1 deficiency in MiaPaCa2.

claims.claim: The inability of MiaPaCa2 cells to produce arginine de novo from citrulline and aspartate may explain why arginine becomes the most limiting substrate for tRNA charging when tRNAGln charging is restored.
claims.source: The inability of MiaPaCa2 cells to produce arginine de novo from citrulline and aspartate may thus explain the observed phenomenon that as soon as tRNAGln charging is restored in these cells, arginine becomes the most limiting substrate for tRNA charging.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that tRNAArg becomes uncharged when tRNAGln is restored, combined with knowledge of MiaPaCa2's arginine auxotrophy.

claims.claim: The rescue of tRNAGln charging by CB-839 in amino-acid-deprived A498 cells leads to a near-complete reversal of amino acid depletion-triggered GCN2 activation.
claims.source: Of note, the observed lack of compensatory tRNA uncharging is mirrored by a near-complete reversal of amino acid depletion-triggered GCN2 activation in A498 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D) in contrast to MEFs (Figure 2E,F) and MiaPaCa2 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F).
claims.evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and 1D showing reversal of GCN2 activation with CB-839 in A498 cells.

claims.claim: CB-839 inhibited proliferation of MEFs, A498, and MiaPaCa2 cells in complete (100% AA) medium.
claims.source: In agreement with published studies, CB-839 inhibited proliferation of MEFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), A498 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H), and MiaPaCa2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I) cells in complete (100% AA) medium.
claims.evidence: Supported by cell proliferation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G-I, consistent with published studies.

claims.claim: Cell lines were not sensitive to glutaminase inhibition when cultured in low AA DMEM (5% AA).
claims.source: However, the cell lines were not sensitive to glutaminase inhibition when cultured in low AA DMEM (5% AA).
claims.evidence: Supported by cell proliferation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G-I showing no growth inhibition with CB-839 in 5% AA medium.

claims.claim: CB-839 treatment enabled proliferation of A498 cells in 5% AA DMEM.
claims.source: In fact, CB-839 treatment enabled proliferation of A498 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H) in 5% AA DMEM.
claims.evidence: Supported by cell proliferation data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H showing increased proliferation with CB-839 in 5% AA medium.

claims.claim: While glutaminase activity is beneficial for fueling biosynthesis and cell proliferation when amino acids are plentiful, it may become a liability for cells that encounter amino-acid-poor environments.
claims.source: Collectively, these observations suggest that while glutaminase activity is beneficial for fueling biosynthesis and cell proliferation when amino acids are plentiful, it may, in fact, become a liability for cells that encounter amino-acid-poor environments.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that glutaminase inhibition is detrimental in nutrient-rich but beneficial in nutrient-poor conditions.

claims.claim: Cells maintain a robust expression of glutaminase regardless of the status of their amino acid supply.
claims.source: Indeed, we detected that cells maintain a robust expression of glutaminase regardless of the status of their amino acid supply (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J), further supporting the key role of glutaminase in depleting charged tRNAGln in amino-acid-poor conditions.
claims.evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1J showing consistent GLS expression across conditions.

claims.claim: CB-839 treatment suppressed the eventual reactivation of mTORC1 upon a prolonged amino acid deprivation in all cell types tested.
claims.source: CB-839 treatment also suppressed the eventual reactivation of mTORC1 upon a prolonged amino acid deprivation in all cell types tested (Figure 2E,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–F), while no effect of CB-839 on mTORC1 activity in presence of amino acids was evident.
claims.evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 2E, 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-F showing reduced mTORC1 reactivation with CB-839.

claims.claim: By restoring charged tRNAGln pools, inhibition of glutaminolysis may bolster adaptive translation in amino-acid-depleted environments, which may deplete the levels of essential amino acids such as methionine and arginine needed to activate mTORC1.
claims.source: One possible explanation of this effect is that by restoring charged tRNAGln pools, inhibition of glutaminolysis may, in fact, bolster adaptive translation in amino-acid-depleted environments. This increase in translation may deplete the levels of essential amino acids such as methionine (Figure 2D) and arginine (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), needed to activate mTORC1.
claims.evidence: Speculative explanation for the observed suppression of mTORC1 reactivation by CB-839.

claims.claim: CB-839 treatment was associated with an increase in ATF4 accumulation in amino-acid-poor conditions across all cellular contexts tested.
claims.source: Intriguingly, CB-839 treatment was associated with an increase in ATF4 accumulation in amino-acid-poor conditions across all cellular contexts tested (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), despite eliciting no further increase in GCN2 phosphorylation.
claims.evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, 1F showing increased ATF4 with CB-839.

claims.claim: ATF4 protein has a half-life of only 1 hr.
claims.source: However, ATF4 protein is also a very short-lived protein with a half-life of only 1 hr (Lassot et al., 2001) – which, paradoxically, makes its accumulation highly dependent on the cellular ability to carry out translation.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Lassot et al., 2001 describing ATF4 half-life.

claims.claim: The increase in ATF4 accumulation in amino-acid-depleted cells upon CB-839 treatment may indicate that restoring tRNAGln charging augments the total cellular capacity for translation.
claims.source: Taking this into account, the increase in ATF4 accumulation in amino-acid-depleted cells upon CB-839 treatment may indicate that restoring tRNAGln charging augments the total cellular capacity for translation – which, in turn, allows cells to accumulate more ATF4.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that ATF4, a short-lived protein, accumulates more with CB-839 treatment.

claims.claim: Glutaminase inhibition markedly increased bulk translation in amino-acid-deprived cells.
claims.source: Indeed, glutaminase inhibition markedly increased bulk translation in amino-acid-deprived cells (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: Supported by OPP incorporation data in Figure 3A showing increased translation with CB-839.

claims.claim: A similar effect on translation was observed with other available GLS inhibitors – BPTES and Compound 968.
claims.source: A similar effect was observed with other available GLS inhibitors – BPTES and Compound 968 (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: Supported by OPP incorporation data in Figure 3B showing increased translation with BPTES and Compound 968.

claims.claim: Supplying L-glutamine at the concentration of 200 μM facilitated translation in amino-acid-deprived cells to an extent similar to that seen upon GLS inhibition.
claims.source: Moreover, supplying L-glutamine at the concentration of 200 μM (which represents 5% of DMEM formulation) facilitated translation in amino-acid-deprived cells to an extent similar to that seen upon GLS inhibition (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: Supported by OPP incorporation data in Figure 3C showing increased translation with glutamine supplementation.

claims.claim: Supplying 10 μM L-methionine had no effect on the overall translation rate in amino-acid-deprived cells.
claims.source: In contrast, supplying 10 μM L-methionine (5% of DMEM formulation) had no effect on the overall translation rate, indicating that translation in amino-acid-deprived cells is hampered specifically by the deficit of charged tRNAGln, which must be resolved before any benefit could be derived from resupplying other limiting amino acids.
claims.evidence: Supported by OPP incorporation data in Figure 3C showing no effect of methionine supplementation.

claims.claim: Translation in amino-acid-deprived cells is hampered specifically by the deficit of charged tRNAGln, which must be resolved before any benefit could be derived from resupplying other limiting amino acids.
claims.source: In contrast, supplying 10 μM L-methionine (5% of DMEM formulation) had no effect on the overall translation rate, indicating that translation in amino-acid-deprived cells is hampered specifically by the deficit of charged tRNAGln, which must be resolved before any benefit could be derived from resupplying other limiting amino acids.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that glutamine but not methionine supplementation rescues translation.

claims.claim: Either glutaminase inhibition or supplementation of exogenous glutamine rescued amino acid withdrawal-associated suppression of translation in MiaPaCa2 and A498 cells.
claims.source: Similarly to the effects observed in MEFs, either glutaminase inhibition or supplementation of exogenous glutamine rescued amino acid withdrawal-associated suppression of translation in MiaPaCa2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and A498 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) cells as well.
claims.evidence: Supported by OPP incorporation data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and 1B showing translation rescue in these cell lines.

claims.claim: The loss of tRNAGln charging is a key limiting factor for new protein synthesis in amino-acid-poor conditions across a variety of cellular contexts.
claims.source: This result indicates that the loss of tRNAGln charging is a key limiting factor for new protein synthesis in amino-acid-poor conditions across a variety of cellular contexts.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that restoring tRNAGln charging rescues translation across multiple cell types.

claims.claim: A 6 hr amino acid deprivation led to a precipitous decline in d2GFP signal, while having no effect on the stable GFP levels.
claims.source: Indeed, a 6 hr amino acid deprivation led to a precipitous decline in d2GFP signal, while having no effect on the stable GFP levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C showing differential effects on GFP and d2GFP.

claims.claim: The decline in d2GFP during amino acid deprivation could not be explained by an increase in clearance of d2GFP from amino-acid-deprived cells.
claims.source: This effect could not be explained by an increase in clearance of d2GFP from amino-acid-deprived cells, as measured by a cycloheximide chase (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D showing no change in d2GFP clearance rate.

claims.claim: Adding CB-839 or 5% L-Gln to amino-acid-deprived cells resulted in an increase in d2GFP accumulation.
claims.source: Consistent with the observed effect on OPP incorporation, adding CB-839 or 5% L-Gln to amino-acid-deprived cells resulted in an increase in d2GFP accumulation (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 3D showing increased d2GFP with CB-839 or glutamine.

claims.claim: ISRIB had no effect on d2GFP accumulation in amino-acid-deprived cells.
claims.source: No such effect was observed when amino-acid-deprived cells were treated with eIF2B activator ISRIB. This suggests that the effect of CB-839 on GFP accumulation is not a consequence of the relief of the phospho-eIF2α-driven translational inhibition.
claims.evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 3D showing no effect of ISRIB on d2GFP.

claims.claim: The effect of CB-839 on d2GFP accumulation is not a consequence of the relief of the phospho-eIF2α-driven translational inhibition.
claims.source: No such effect was observed when amino-acid-deprived cells were treated with eIF2B activator ISRIB. This suggests that the effect of CB-839 on GFP accumulation is not a consequence of the relief of the phospho-eIF2α-driven translational inhibition.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that ISRIB does not affect d2GFP accumulation.

claims.claim: CB-839 treatment did not prevent the clearance of d2GFP from cells in which translation was arrested with cycloheximide.
claims.source: Finally, CB-839 treatment did not prevent the clearance of d2GFP from cells in which translation was arrested with cycloheximide, suggesting that CB-839-driven increase in d2GFP was not due to a non-specific interference of CB-839 with the protein degradation machinery (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 3D showing d2GFP clearance with cycloheximide regardless of CB-839.

claims.claim: CB-839-driven increase in d2GFP was not due to a non-specific interference of CB-839 with the protein degradation machinery.
claims.source: Finally, CB-839 treatment did not prevent the clearance of d2GFP from cells in which translation was arrested with cycloheximide, suggesting that CB-839-driven increase in d2GFP was not due to a non-specific interference of CB-839 with the protein degradation machinery (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that CB-839 does not affect d2GFP clearance when translation is blocked.

claims.claim: IgG yield by A20 cells was reduced when amino acids were limiting.
claims.source: As expected, IgG yield by A20 cells was reduced when amino acids were limiting, yet a concomitant inhibition of glutaminase with CB-839 restored it to a level comparable to that seen in amino-acid-replete cells (Figure 3E,F).
claims.evidence: Supported by dot blot data in Figure 3E and quantification in Figure 3F showing reduced IgG in low amino acid conditions.

claims.claim: Inhibition of glutaminase with CB-839 restored IgG yield in amino-acid-limited A20 cells to a level comparable to that seen in amino-acid-replete cells.
claims.source: As expected, IgG yield by A20 cells was reduced when amino acids were limiting, yet a concomitant inhibition of glutaminase with CB-839 restored it to a level comparable to that seen in amino-acid-replete cells (Figure 3E,F).
claims.evidence: Supported by dot blot data in Figure 3E and quantification in Figure 3F showing IgG restoration with CB-839.

claims.claim: The selective loss of charged tRNAGln limits translation in amino-acid-depleted cells, which can be counteracted by adding exogenous glutamine or blocking glutamine consumption in a glutaminolysis reaction.
claims.source: Taken together, these results indicate that the selective loss of charged tRNAGln limits translation in amino-acid-depleted cells, which can be counteracted by adding exogenous glutamine or blocking glutamine consumption in a glutaminolysis reaction.
claims.evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing that glutamine supplementation or glutaminase inhibition rescues translation.

claims.claim: There are 68 proteins in the human proteome that contain uninterrupted tracts of 10 or more glutamine residues, known as polyglutamine, or polyQ, tracts.
claims.source: However, there are 68 proteins in the human proteome that contain uninterrupted tracts of 10 or more glutamine residues, known as polyglutamine, or polyQ, tracts.
claims.evidence: Factual statement about the human proteome, likely based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: PolyQ tracts are thought to provide flexibility within multisubunit protein complexes.
claims.source: PolyQ tracts are thought to provide flexibility within multisubunit protein complexes (Tóth-Petróczy et al., 2008) as well as to be functionally involved in phase separation phenomena (Fiumara et al., 2010; Vitalis et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Tóth-Petróczy et al., 2008.

claims.claim: PolyQ tracts are functionally involved in phase separation phenomena.
claims.source: PolyQ tracts are thought to provide flexibility within multisubunit protein complexes (Tóth-Petróczy et al., 2008) as well as to be functionally involved in phase separation phenomena (Fiumara et al., 2010; Vitalis et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Fiumara et al., 2010 and Vitalis et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Expansions of polyQ tracts in select proteins underlie the pathology of several neurodegenerative diseases including Huntington's disease and spinocerebellar ataxia.
claims.source: In addition, expansions of polyQ tracts in select proteins underlie the pathology of a several neurodegenerative diseases including Huntington's disease and spinocerebellar ataxia (Lieberman et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Lieberman et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Culturing MiaPaCa2 cells in amino-acid-depleted conditions (5% AA) significantly reduced the levels of several polyQ proteins, including TATA-box binding protein (TBP), mediator complex subunit 12 (MED12), core binding factor α1 (CBPα1), and CREB-binding protein (CBP).
claims.source: Indeed, culturing MiaPaCa2 cells in amino-acid-depleted conditions (5% AA) significantly reduced the levels of several polyQ proteins, including TATA-box binding protein (TBP), mediator complex subunit 12 (MED12), core binding factor α1 (CBPα1), and CREB-binding protein (CBP).
claims.evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 4A showing reduced polyQ protein levels in 5% AA.

claims.claim: Proteins lacking polyQ tracts showed little to no depletion in 5% AA, indicating that polyQ-containing proteins are particularly sensitive to amino acid deficit.
claims.source: In contrast, proteins lacking polyQ tracts showed little to no depletion in 5% AA, indicating that polyQ-containing proteins are particularly sensitive to amino acid deficit (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 4A showing differential effects on polyQ vs non-polyQ proteins.

claims.claim: Supplementing amino-acid-depleted medium with either CB-839 or glutamine restored the levels of all four polyQ-containing proteins tested.
claims.source: Furthermore, supplementing amino-acid-depleted medium with either CB-839 or glutamine restored the levels of all four polyQ-containing proteins tested, suggesting that levels of polyQ proteins can be modulated by changes in the availability of glutamine for translation.
claims.evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 4A showing restoration of polyQ protein levels with CB-839 or glutamine.

claims.claim: Levels of polyQ proteins can be modulated by changes in the availability of glutamine for translation.
claims.source: Furthermore, supplementing amino-acid-depleted medium with either CB-839 or glutamine restored the levels of all four polyQ-containing proteins tested, suggesting that levels of polyQ proteins can be modulated by changes in the availability of glutamine for translation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that glutamine availability affects polyQ protein levels.

claims.claim: Exposing cells to limiting amino acid conditions markedly suppressed incorporation of labeled uridine into nascent RNA.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that exposing cells to limiting amino acid conditions markedly suppressed incorporation of labeled uridine into nascent RNA, which could be partially restored by CB-839 or added glutamine, thus mirroring the effect these conditions had on polyQ protein levels (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: Supported by 5-EU incorporation data in Figure 4B showing reduced RNA synthesis in amino acid-limited conditions.

claims.claim: The suppression of RNA synthesis in amino acid-limited conditions could be partially restored by CB-839 or added glutamine.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that exposing cells to limiting amino acid conditions markedly suppressed incorporation of labeled uridine into nascent RNA, which could be partially restored by CB-839 or added glutamine, thus mirroring the effect these conditions had on polyQ protein levels (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: Supported by 5-EU incorporation data in Figure 4B showing partial restoration of RNA synthesis with CB-839 or glutamine.

claims.claim: shRNA constructs targeting human GLS resulted in a significant rescue of both polyQ protein expression and labeled uridine incorporation in amino-acid-depleted cells.
claims.source: Similarly to the effects observed with CB-839 and with exogenous glutamine supplementation, shRNA constructs targeting human GLS, but not control shRNAs, resulted in a significant rescue of both polyQ protein expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) as well as of labeled uridine incorporation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) in amino-acid-depleted cells.
claims.evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and 5-EU incorporation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Glutaminase inhibition did not increase the size of nucleotide triphosphate pools in amino-acid-depleted cells.
claims.source: Importantly, glutaminase inhibition did not increase the size of nucleotide triphosphate pools in amino-acid-depleted cells, indicating that its effect on RNA synthesis is unlikely to be explained by increased nucleotide availability under these conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F showing no increase in NTP pools with CB-839.

claims.claim: The effect of glutaminase inhibition on RNA synthesis is unlikely to be explained by increased nucleotide availability.
claims.source: Importantly, glutaminase inhibition did not increase the size of nucleotide triphosphate pools in amino-acid-depleted cells, indicating that its effect on RNA synthesis is unlikely to be explained by increased nucleotide availability under these conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that NTP pools do not increase with glutaminase inhibition.

claims.claim: The presence of polyQ tracts within transcriptional regulators may represent an amino-acid-sensing adaptation that allows a cell to modulate transcriptional output in response to changes in amino acid availability.
claims.source: Taken together, these observations raise the possibility that the presence of polyQ tracts within transcriptional regulators may represent an amino-acid-sensing adaptation that allows a cell to modulate transcriptional output in response to changes in amino acid availability.
claims.evidence: Speculative interpretation of the collective observations about polyQ proteins and transcription.

claims.claim: Even though both glutamine-poor and leucine-poor conditions equivalently inhibited bulk translation, only glutamine-poor formulations led to a significant depletion of polyQ proteins.
claims.source: Even though both glutamine-poor and leucine-poor conditions equivalently inhibited bulk translation, only glutamine-poor formulations led to a significant depletion of polyQ proteins (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: Supported by puromycin incorporation and western blot data in Figure 4C showing differential effects of glutamine vs leucine depletion.

claims.claim: Depletion of glutamine specifically, and not the inhibition of translation associated with the depletion of a different amino acid, is responsible for the observed decline in polyQ protein levels.
claims.source: Taken together, these observations indicate that depletion of glutamine specifically, and not the inhibition of translation associated with the depletion of a different amino acid, is responsible for the observed decline in polyQ protein levels.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that only glutamine depletion, not leucine depletion, affects polyQ protein levels.

claims.claim: Recombinant TBP with an intact polyQ tract behaved similarly to endogenous TBP protein – its levels declined precipitously in amino-acid-depleted conditions and were fully restored by CB-839.
claims.source: As expected, recombinant TBP with an intact polyQ tract behaved similarly to endogenous TBP protein – that is, its levels declined precipitously in amino-acid-depleted conditions and were fully restored by CB-839 (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 4D showing similar behavior of recombinant and endogenous TBP.

claims.claim: Levels of recombinant TBP lacking the polyQ tract (ΔpolyQ TBP-HA) showed no decline upon amino acid depletion.
claims.source: In contrast, levels of recombinant TBP lacking the polyQ tract (ΔpolyQ TBP-HA) showed no decline upon amino acid depletion.
claims.evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 4D showing stable levels of ΔpolyQ TBP-HA.

claims.claim: The polyQ tract is required for the sensitivity of TBP to amino acid depletion.
claims.source: Taken together, these data indicate that the polyQ tract is required for the sensitivity of TBP to amino acid depletion.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that removing the polyQ tract eliminates TBP's sensitivity to amino acid depletion.

claims.claim: PolyQ-GFP-expressing cells accumulated markedly less fluorescence in amino-acid-depleted than in complete medium.
claims.source: In contrast to control GFP-expressing cells, in which the amount of fluorescence accumulation over the course of 6 hr was not affected by the absence of extracellular amino acids, PolyQ-GFP-expressing cells accumulated markedly less fluorescence in amino-acid-depleted than in complete medium (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 4F showing reduced PolyQ-GFP accumulation in amino acid-depleted conditions.

claims.claim: The reduced PolyQ-GFP accumulation in amino-acid-deprived cells could not be attributed to the decreased half-life of PolyQ-GFP protein.
claims.source: This effect could not be attributed to the decreased half-life of PolyQ-GFP protein in amino-acid-deprived cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G showing no change in PolyQ-GFP half-life.

claims.claim: Both CB-839 and supplementing additional glutamine facilitated PolyQ-GFP accumulation in amino-acid-deprived cells.
claims.source: Importantly, both CB-839 and supplementing additional glutamine facilitated PolyQ-GFP accumulation in amino-acid-deprived cells, providing additional evidence that restoring charged tRNAGln pools may ameliorate the defect in polyQ protein synthesis in an amino-acid-limited state (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 4G showing increased PolyQ-GFP with CB-839 or glutamine.

claims.claim: Restoring charged tRNAGln pools may ameliorate the defect in polyQ protein synthesis in an amino-acid-limited state.
claims.source: Importantly, both CB-839 and supplementing additional glutamine facilitated PolyQ-GFP accumulation in amino-acid-deprived cells, providing additional evidence that restoring charged tRNAGln pools may ameliorate the defect in polyQ protein synthesis in an amino-acid-limited state (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that treatments that restore tRNAGln charging improve polyQ protein synthesis.

claims.claim: An RNAi-mediated depletion of tRNAGln, or an overexpression of tRNAAla, leads to a decreased translational fidelity of polyQ tracts in human huntingtin transcript, resulting in a −1 ribosomal frameshift.
claims.source: A recent study of translation of polyglutamine-containing human huntingtin transcript has revealed that an RNAi-mediated depletion of tRNAGln, or an overexpression of tRNAAla, leads to a decreased translational fidelity of its polyQ tract, resulting in a −1 ribosomal frameshift from a (CAG)n into a (GCA)n frame, and consequently, formation of a polyalanine-containing polypeptide product (Girstmair et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Girstmair et al., 2013.

claims.claim: While PolyQ−1-GFP-expressing MEFs cultured in complete medium expressed no GFP, amino acid deprivation triggered a marked GFP accumulation.
claims.source: Indeed, while PolyQ−1-GFP-expressing MEFs cultured in complete medium expressed no GFP, amino acid deprivation triggered a marked GFP accumulation. This effect was completely blocked by CB-839 (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 5B showing GFP accumulation in amino acid-deprived conditions.

claims.claim: CB-839 completely blocked the amino acid deprivation-triggered GFP accumulation in PolyQ−1-GFP-expressing MEFs.
claims.source: Indeed, while PolyQ−1-GFP-expressing MEFs cultured in complete medium expressed no GFP, amino acid deprivation triggered a marked GFP accumulation. This effect was completely blocked by CB-839 (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 5B showing no GFP accumulation with CB-839 treatment.

claims.claim: Growth of MiaPaCa2 cells in 5% AA medium triggered GFP accumulation in PolyQ−1-GFP-expressing cells.
claims.source: To test whether human cells also exhibited a loss of translational fidelity, MiaPaCa2 cells were cultured in 5% AA DMEM for 24 hr. Growth in 5% AA medium triggered GFP accumulation as well (Figure 5C), and this accumulation was also suppressed by CB-839 (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) or by adding exogenous glutamine (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by FACS data in Figure 5C showing GFP accumulation in 5% AA medium.

claims.claim: GFP accumulation in PolyQ−1-GFP-expressing MiaPaCa2 cells was suppressed by CB-839 or by adding exogenous glutamine.

claims.claim: Cells have the capacity to maintain pools of charged tRNAs during interruptions in extracellular amino acid supply.
claims.source: The present work demonstrates that cells have the capacity to maintain pools of charged tRNAs during interruptions in extracellular amino acid supply.
claims.evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing maintained tRNA charging for most amino acids during amino acid deprivation.

claims.claim: The ability to maintain a charged tRNA compartment in amino-acid-deprived cells requires lysosomal function.
claims.source: The ability to maintain a charged tRNA compartment in amino-acid-deprived cells requires lysosomal function, which is consistent with the established role of the lysosome as a critical source of amino acids in a nutrient-limited state.
claims.evidence: Supported by data showing that bafilomycin A1 prevents maintenance of tRNA charging, consistent with known lysosomal function.

claims.claim: Adaptive translation over time results in a selective depletion of tRNAGln charging that reduces the net translation.
claims.source: Our work further reveals that adaptive translation over time results in a selective depletion of tRNAGln charging that reduces the net translation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from observations showing progressive tRNAGln depletion and translation decline during amino acid deprivation.

claims.source: This reduction in translation does not occur because cells cannot either recycle glutamine from lysosome-degraded proteins or take up sufficient extracellular glutamine when the vascular delivery of amino acids is compromised.

claims.source: This indicates that even though glutaminase inhibition suppresses growth when amino acids are abundant, it facilitates translation and even cell proliferation when amino acid supply is limited.
claims.evidence: Supported by cell proliferation data showing differential effects of glutaminase inhibition in nutrient-rich vs nutrient-poor conditions.

claims.claim: Amino acid depletion is associated with the loss of translational fidelity among polyglutamine-containing transcripts, which takes place in discrete areas of solid tumors in vivo.

claims.evidence: Supported by frameshift reporter data in vitro and xenograft immunohistochemistry data in vivo.

results.result: Amino acid deprivation in MEFs causes initial mTORC1 inactivation followed by reactivation during prolonged deprivation. This reactivation is suppressed by bafilomycin A1, indicating dependence on lysosomal amino acid supply.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 are well-supported by western blot data in Figure 1A showing temporal changes in phospho-S6K1 levels and the effect of bafilomycin A1. The interpretation is consistent with established knowledge about lysosomal function in amino acid recycling and is supported by appropriate citations.

results.result: GCN2 activation during amino acid deprivation is gradual and correlates with progressive decline in translation. However, translation continues at reduced levels even after 6 hours of amino acid deprivation, indicating ongoing adaptive translation.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C8 are supported by western blot data showing GCN2 phosphorylation kinetics (Figure 1A) and OPP incorporation data demonstrating declining but persistent translation (Figure 1B). The comparison with cycloheximide provides appropriate negative control for complete translation inhibition.

results.result: ISRIB treatment has minimal effect on translation suppression during amino acid deprivation, despite blocking ATF4 accumulation and increasing eIF2α phosphorylation. This indicates that GCN2-mediated eIF2α phosphorylation is not the major cause of translation suppression.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C12 are supported by OPP incorporation and western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B. The logic is sound: if eIF2α phosphorylation were the primary mechanism, ISRIB should rescue translation. However, the interpretation could benefit from additional controls to rule out off-target effects of ISRIB.

results.result: During amino acid deprivation, tRNAGln becomes selectively uncharged while tRNAs for Met, Leu, Arg, and Val remain charged. This selective depletion occurs despite maintained charging of other tRNAs even when their corresponding free amino acid levels decline.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C17 are well-supported by tRNA charging assay data (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-E) and mass spectrometry data. The statistical significance is reported (p<0.05 at 1hr, p<0.001 at 6hr for tRNAGln). The observation that other tRNAs remain charged despite reduced free amino acid levels is particularly important and well-documented.

results.result: Bafilomycin A1 treatment prevents maintenance of tRNAVal and tRNAMet charging during amino acid deprivation but does not further increase GCN2 phosphorylation, suggesting that uncharged tRNAGln alone may saturate GCN2 activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C19 are supported by tRNA charging data (Figure 1D) and western blot data (Figure 1A). However, C20 is speculative about GCN2 saturation. While the speculation is reasonable, it lacks direct experimental validation of GCN2's tRNA-sensing capacity limits.

results.result: Translation inhibitors (cycloheximide and L-valinol) rapidly restore tRNAGln charging in amino acid-deprived cells, indicating that tRNAGln continues to be charged but is rapidly consumed in protein synthesis. This suggests that neither glutamine synthesis nor protein degradation is sufficient to maintain tRNAGln charging.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C23 are well-supported by tRNA charging data (Figure 1E-F) showing rapid restoration of tRNAGln charging upon translation inhibition. The on-target activity of L-valinol is confirmed by loss of tRNAVal charging. C24's inference is logical but could benefit from direct measurement of glutamine synthesis rates.

results.result: Northern hybridization-based tRNA charging assay confirms selective uncharging of tRNAGln during amino acid deprivation, with partial recovery upon L-valinol treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C26 are supported by northern blot data (Figure 1G) that independently validates the periodate-based assay results. This orthogonal validation strengthens confidence in the selective tRNAGln depletion finding.

results.result: In chronic low amino acid conditions (5% AA medium), tRNAGln charging is almost completely lost while other tRNAs remain charged, accompanied by increased GCN2 phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C28 are supported by tRNA charging data (Figure 1H) and western blot data (Figure 1I) with appropriate statistical analysis (p=0.0011). This demonstrates that selective tRNAGln depletion occurs in physiologically relevant chronic amino acid limitation, not just acute deprivation.

results.result: Selective loss of tRNAGln charging during amino acid deprivation occurs in both proliferating and quiescent MEFs, indicating independence from proliferative status.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C31 are supported by western blot and tRNA charging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F-G. This control experiment appropriately addresses whether the phenomenon is specific to proliferating cells or represents a general cellular response to amino acid limitation.

results.result: CHARGE-seq analysis reveals that tRNAGln isodecoders (CAG and CAA) are the sole cytosolic tRNAs that become uncharged during amino acid deprivation. Glutaminase inhibitor CB-839 rescues tRNAGln charging but causes compensatory uncharging of tRNAMet, suggesting tRNAMet may be the second-most limiting tRNA in MEFs.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C35 are well-supported by comprehensive CHARGE-seq data (Figure 2C) covering 49 of 50 cytosolic tRNA isodecoders. The compensatory uncharging of tRNAMet is clearly demonstrated. However, C36 is speculative about tRNAMet being second-most limiting, though the speculation is reasonable given the data.

results.result: Glutaminase inhibition has only marginal effect on GCN2 phosphorylation in amino acid-deprived MEFs.
results.evaluation: Claim C37 is supported by western blot data (Figure 2E-F) showing minimal change in GCN2 phosphorylation with CB-839 treatment. This is consistent with the compensatory uncharging of tRNAMet maintaining GCN2 activation.

results.result: Different cell types show distinct patterns of compensatory tRNA uncharging when tRNAGln is restored: A498 cells show no compensatory uncharging and complete GCN2 reversal, while MiaPaCa2 cells show tRNAArg uncharging due to ASS1 deficiency. This indicates cell-type-specific amino acid metabolism dictates tRNA limitation patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C44 are supported by tRNA charging data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-D) and western blot data across multiple cell lines. The explanation for MiaPaCa2's tRNAArg depletion is well-supported by citation to Singh et al., 2019 documenting ASS1 deficiency. The cell-type specificity is an important finding demonstrating metabolic context dependence.

results.result: CB-839 inhibits cell proliferation in complete medium but enables proliferation in amino acid-limited conditions, particularly in A498 cells. Cells maintain robust glutaminase expression regardless of amino acid availability, suggesting glutaminase activity becomes detrimental in amino acid-poor environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C49 are supported by cell proliferation data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G-I) and western blot data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J). The paradoxical effect of glutaminase inhibition in different nutrient contexts is well-documented and represents an important finding about metabolic adaptation.

results.result: CB-839 suppresses mTORC1 reactivation during prolonged amino acid deprivation across all cell types tested. This may occur because restoring tRNAGln charging increases translation, depleting essential amino acids needed for mTORC1 activation.
results.evaluation: Claim C50 is well-supported by western blot data (Figure 2E-F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-F) showing consistent suppression of mTORC1 reactivation. However, C51 is speculative about the mechanism. While the proposed mechanism is plausible and supported by some data (Figure 2D), direct measurement of essential amino acid depletion rates would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: CB-839 treatment increases ATF4 accumulation in amino acid-poor conditions without further increasing GCN2 phosphorylation. Given ATF4's short half-life (1 hr), this suggests that restoring tRNAGln charging augments overall translational capacity.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 are supported by western blot data (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, 1F) and citation for ATF4 half-life (Lassot et al., 2001). The inference in C54 is logical: increased ATF4 despite unchanged GCN2 phosphorylation suggests enhanced translation capacity. However, direct measurement of ATF4 synthesis rates would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Glutaminase inhibition or glutamine supplementation markedly increases bulk translation in amino acid-deprived cells, while methionine supplementation has no effect. This indicates translation is specifically limited by tRNAGln charging deficit, which must be resolved before other amino acids can benefit translation.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59 are well-supported by OPP incorporation data (Figure 3A-C) showing consistent effects across multiple glutaminase inhibitors and with glutamine supplementation. The specificity is demonstrated by lack of effect with methionine. This is a key finding establishing tRNAGln as the primary translational bottleneck.

results.result: Glutaminase inhibition or glutamine supplementation rescues translation suppression in MiaPaCa2 and A498 cells, indicating that tRNAGln charging is a key limiting factor for protein synthesis across diverse cellular contexts.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 are supported by OPP incorporation data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B) demonstrating generalizability across cell types. This strengthens the conclusion that tRNAGln limitation is a fundamental constraint in amino acid-poor conditions.

results.result: Using destabilized d2GFP reporter, amino acid deprivation causes precipitous decline in d2GFP but not stable GFP. CB-839 or glutamine supplementation restores d2GFP accumulation, while ISRIB has no effect. This demonstrates that restoring tRNAGln charging enhances functional protein production independent of eIF2α phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C68 are well-supported by FACS data (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-D) and cycloheximide chase experiments. The use of d2GFP as a reporter for ongoing translation is appropriate given its short half-life. Controls with ISRIB and cycloheximide appropriately rule out alternative mechanisms.

results.result: In A20 B-cell lymphoma cells, IgG secretion is reduced in amino acid-limited conditions but restored to normal levels by glutaminase inhibition. This demonstrates that selective tRNAGln depletion limits translation in specialized protein-producing cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 are supported by dot blot data (Figure 3E-F) showing IgG secretion levels. This experiment in a specialized secretory cell type strengthens the physiological relevance of the findings. The biomass normalization is appropriate for comparing secretion rates.

results.result: There are 68 proteins in the human proteome containing polyQ tracts (≥10 glutamines). These tracts provide flexibility in protein complexes, participate in phase separation, and when expanded, cause neurodegenerative diseases.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 are supported by established knowledge and appropriate citations (Tóth-Petróczy et al., 2008; Fiumara et al., 2010; Vitalis et al., 2007; Lieberman et al., 2019). This provides important context for the subsequent experiments on polyQ protein sensitivity.

results.result: Amino acid limitation (5% AA) selectively depletes polyQ-containing transcription factors (TBP, MED12, CBFα1, CBP) while sparing non-polyQ proteins. CB-839 or glutamine supplementation restores polyQ protein levels, indicating they are sensitive to glutamine availability for translation.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 are well-supported by western blot data (Figure 4A) showing differential effects on polyQ vs non-polyQ proteins. The restoration with CB-839 or glutamine establishes the mechanism. This is a novel and important finding linking tRNAGln availability to polyQ protein expression.

results.result: Amino acid limitation suppresses RNA synthesis, which is partially restored by CB-839 or glutamine. This effect is confirmed by shRNA-mediated GLS knockdown and is not due to increased nucleotide availability, suggesting polyQ transcription factor depletion reduces transcriptional output.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C84 are supported by 5-EU incorporation data (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) and mass spectrometry data ruling out nucleotide pool changes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F). The shRNA validation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) strengthens confidence in on-target effects. The mechanistic link to polyQ transcription factors is logical but somewhat indirect.

results.result: PolyQ tracts in transcriptional regulators may represent an amino acid-sensing adaptation allowing cells to modulate transcriptional output in response to amino acid availability.
results.evaluation: Claim C85 is explicitly speculative ('raise the possibility'). While the hypothesis is interesting and consistent with the data, it lacks direct experimental validation. Testing this would require evolutionary analysis, gain/loss of function experiments with polyQ tracts, and demonstration of adaptive benefit.

results.result: Glutamine-specific depletion, not general translation inhibition, causes polyQ protein depletion. Both glutamine-poor and leucine-poor conditions inhibit translation equally, but only glutamine depletion reduces polyQ protein levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 are supported by puromycin incorporation and western blot data (Figure 4C) demonstrating equivalent translation inhibition but differential effects on polyQ proteins. This control experiment is critical for establishing specificity to glutamine rather than general translation suppression.

results.result: The polyQ tract is required for TBP sensitivity to amino acid depletion. Recombinant TBP with intact polyQ tract behaves like endogenous TBP (depleted by amino acid limitation, restored by CB-839), while ΔpolyQ TBP shows no depletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 are well-supported by western blot data (Figure 4D) comparing wild-type and ΔpolyQ TBP. This gain/loss of function experiment directly demonstrates that the polyQ tract confers sensitivity to amino acid limitation. This is strong mechanistic evidence.

results.result: PolyQ-GFP reporter accumulates less fluorescence in amino acid-depleted conditions compared to control GFP. This is not due to decreased protein stability but is rescued by CB-839 or glutamine supplementation, indicating that adding a polyQ tract confers sensitivity to tRNAGln availability.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C94 are supported by FACS data (Figure 4F-G) and cycloheximide chase experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G). The control with stable GFP and the half-life measurements appropriately rule out alternative explanations. This demonstrates sufficiency of polyQ tract to confer amino acid sensitivity.

results.result: Prior work by Girstmair et al. (2013) showed that tRNAGln depletion or tRNAAla overexpression causes -1 ribosomal frameshifting on huntingtin polyQ tracts, producing polyalanine products.
results.evaluation: Claim C95 accurately cites prior work (Girstmair et al., 2013) that provides the conceptual foundation for the frameshift reporter experiments. This is appropriate background for the subsequent experiments.

results.result: Amino acid deprivation triggers GFP accumulation in PolyQ-1-GFP frameshift reporter in both MEFs and MiaPaCa2 cells, which is completely blocked by CB-839 or glutamine supplementation. No frameshifting occurs in complete medium.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C100 are well-supported by FACS data (Figure 5B-C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) showing frameshift-dependent GFP expression specifically in amino acid-depleted conditions. The complete suppression by CB-839 or glutamine establishes the mechanism. This is a novel finding demonstrating translational fidelity loss.

results.result: Frameshift-dependent GFP expression occurs in MC38 cells and correlates with the extent of amino acid depletion (10% vs 5% AA).
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C102 are supported by FACS data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C) demonstrating generalizability to another cell line and dose-response relationship. This strengthens the conclusion that frameshifting is a general response to amino acid limitation.

results.result: ISRIB has no effect on frameshift-dependent GFP expression, indicating the frameshifting is not orchestrated by eIF2α phosphorylation-associated stress response.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C104 are supported by FACS data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D). This control appropriately rules out the eIF2α phosphorylation pathway as the mechanism for frameshifting, consistent with earlier findings that ISRIB doesn't rescue translation suppression.

results.result: Across multiple cell types, amino acid depletion causes frameshifting on polyQ tracts. Glutaminase inhibition or glutamine supplementation prevents this frameshifting, implicating tRNAGln deficit as the mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C107 are supported by FACS data across multiple cell types showing consistent frameshifting and its prevention by treatments that restore tRNAGln charging. The mechanistic link to tRNAGln is well-established through the pattern of interventions that prevent frameshifting.

results.result: Only amino acid depletion, not other cellular stresses (glucose depletion, oxidative stress, ER stress, osmotic stress), triggers frameshifting on polyQ tracts, indicating amino acid deficit is a specific trigger.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C109 are supported by FACS data (Figure 5D) testing multiple stress conditions. This specificity control is important for establishing that frameshifting is not a general stress response but specifically linked to amino acid availability.

results.result: Luc-1-GFP control reporter shows minimal frameshifting compared to PolyQ-1-GFP, and PolyQ-1-GFP shows greater frameshifting in glutamine-poor than leucine-poor conditions. This demonstrates that polyQ tracts specifically promote frameshifting in response to glutamine depletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C113 are supported by FACS data (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) comparing PolyQ and Luc reporters and testing amino acid specificity. These controls are critical for establishing that the polyQ tract itself promotes frameshifting and that the effect is glutamine-specific.

results.result: Frameshifting is reversible: GFP levels decline when amino acid-depleted cells are re-fed with complete medium, demonstrating that frameshifting is contingent on amino acid deficit.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C115 are supported by FACS data (Figure 5F) showing GFP decline after re-feeding. This reversibility experiment is important for demonstrating that frameshifting is a dynamic response to nutrient availability rather than a permanent change.

results.result: Translation of polyQ-containing transcripts is prone to frameshifting specifically in response to amino acid deficit (not other stresses) across diverse cellular contexts, and can be prevented by restoring tRNAGln charging.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C117 synthesize findings from multiple experiments across cell types and conditions. The conclusions are well-supported by the comprehensive data showing specificity to amino acid depletion, generalizability across cell types, and mechanistic link to tRNAGln.

results.result: In MiaPaCa2 xenografts, multiple nests of GFP+ cells (10-100 cells) are observed in PolyQ-1-GFP tumors but not controls. These are unlikely to be clonal outgrowths since no GFP+ clones emerge in vitro, indicating frameshifting occurs in discrete areas within solid tumors in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C121 are supported by immunohistochemistry data (Figure 6A) and clonal density experiments. The control experiment ruling out constitutive GFP+ clones is appropriate. This demonstrates physiological relevance by showing frameshifting occurs in vivo in nutrient-poor tumor regions.

results.result: The proportion of GFP+ cells in xenografts peaks at week 3 and declines by week 5, suggesting either selection against GFP+ cells or reduced mistranslation as tumors mature.
results.evaluation: Claim C122 is supported by FACS data (Figure 6B) showing temporal changes. However, C123 is speculative about the mechanism. The two proposed explanations (selection vs. reduced mistranslation) are plausible but not distinguished experimentally. Additional experiments would be needed to determine which mechanism is operative.

results.result: Cells can maintain charged tRNA pools during amino acid deprivation through lysosomal function, consistent with the lysosome's role as an amino acid source in nutrient limitation.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C125 synthesize findings from multiple experiments showing maintained tRNA charging for most amino acids and its dependence on lysosomal function (bafilomycin A1 experiments). This conclusion is well-supported and consistent with established knowledge.

results.result: Adaptive translation causes selective tRNAGln depletion that reduces translation. This occurs not from inability to recycle or uptake glutamine, but from glutaminase-mediated conversion to glutamate. Glutaminase inhibition restores tRNAGln charging and translation in amino acid-depleted cells, with opposite effects in nutrient-rich vs. nutrient-poor conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C130 synthesize the major mechanistic findings. The conclusions are well-supported by comprehensive data showing: (1) selective tRNAGln depletion, (2) ongoing charging but rapid consumption, (3) rescue by glutaminase inhibition, and (4) context-dependent effects on proliferation. This represents the core mechanistic insight of the paper.

results.result: Amino acid limitation-associated tRNAGln depletion causes collective depletion of polyQ-containing transcription factors and reduces transcriptional output.
results.evaluation: Claim C131 is supported by western blot data showing polyQ transcription factor depletion and 5-EU incorporation data showing reduced RNA synthesis. The causal link between polyQ protein depletion and reduced transcription is logical but somewhat indirect - it would be strengthened by rescue experiments showing that maintaining polyQ protein levels prevents transcriptional decline.

results.result: Comparative sequence analysis shows polyQ tract position varies among orthologs, suggesting the presence rather than location is functionally important. This raises the possibility that polyQ tracts serve a nutrient-sensing function by modulating protein levels in response to amino acid availability.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C133 are supported by citation to Schaefer et al., 2012. However, C134 is explicitly speculative ('raise the possibility'). While the hypothesis is interesting and consistent with the data, it lacks direct experimental validation of adaptive benefit or evolutionary selection for this function.

results.result: Amino acid depletion causes loss of translational fidelity on polyQ-containing transcripts, which occurs in discrete areas of solid tumors in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claim C135 synthesizes findings from frameshift reporter experiments in vitro and xenograft experiments in vivo. The conclusion is well-supported by comprehensive data demonstrating frameshifting in multiple cell types in culture and in tumor tissue sections.
